newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN GDP SEEN RISING BUT JOBS MKT WON'T BENEFIT.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN GDP SEEN RISING BUT JOBS MKT WON'T BENEFIT.

text.p: The German economy will pick up steam in 1997 and 1998 as companies sell more goods abroad but unemployment, now at 11.2 percent, will come down only slowly, a Reuter poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
Economists at 27 banks expect Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by 2.2 percent in 1997 on average and by 2.7 percent in 1998.
The extent of 1997 GDP growth is crucial to Bonn's efforts to qualify for the European single currency and the analysts' prediction is below the government growth forecast of 2.5 pct.

Bonn is aiming for a budget deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997, just below the three percent ceiling set for countries wishing to join the euro. That outlook hinges in part on the assumption that GDP will grow by 2.5 percent.

Economists said 1997 growth, following a modest rise of 1.4 percent in 1996, will be driven mainly by exports because the mark's depreciation against the dollar and major European currencies has made German products cheaper to sell abroad.
"The main motor of expected growth is exports," said Eberhardt Unger, an economist at BfG Bank in Frankfurt.
"The U.S. dollar and British pound have strengthened by 30 percent against the mark compared with their lows in 1995. That has given a tremendous boost to the competitiveness of the German economy."

Europe's economic juggernaut, the world's third largest exporter after the U.S. and Japan, will also benefit from a rise in world growth which will fuel demand for the fruits of German industry like cars, machine tools, industrial plant and equipment, and chemicals, economists say.
But joblessness, which in February hit its highest level since Hitler's rise to power in 1933, will stay stubbornly high.
The unemployment rate is expected to stagnate at 11.1 percent in 1997 and ease only slightly to 10.6 percent in 1998, the survey shows.

The rise in exports will feed through into higher domestic investment during 1997 but the jobs market will not benefit much because most of the investment will be geared to rationalisation and replacing existing equipment rather than expanding capacity, economists say.
"That's not the kind of investment that creates jobs on a big scale," said Mathias Haffner, an economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in Frankfurt.
Meanwhile domestic consumption will remain restrained by fear of unemployment and by general confusion among consumers about the outcome of political wrangling over planned tax reforms.
"With all this back and forth about the reforms it's unclear what shape they will take and when they will take effect," said Thomas Kull at Westdeutsche Landesbank.
The government plans to cut 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes to boost investment, but it may decide to raise value added tax or petrol tax to help finance the package.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) oppose some of the measures and have the power to block them through their majority in the Bundesrat or upper house of the federal parliament.

The ruling coalition of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), the Bavarian sister party CSU and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) are scheduled to meet the SPD for more discussions on the reforms on Wednesday after little progress was made in talks last Tuesday.

The weak construction sector is also expected to dampen growth and keep unemployment high, with German builders increasingly under pressure from foreign competition and declining building investment, economists say.
